items.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000
items.q: We had occasional visits from Eddie Condon, Ernie Anderson, Joe’s brother, was his manager

ctx.x: Is that good? Okay. I’m just going to pick up from where we were. It seems like a pretty mature attitude on your part at that time to know that maybe you couldn’t make a living as a musician?

Monk, I don’t know that I really ever thought about it to tell you the truth. In those days I went off to college and in college here I didn’t play. We had occasional visits from Eddie Condon, Ernie Anderson, Joe’s brother, was his manager, and he came up here several times and other big bands and I saw that. But I was kind of out of it except for playing records and so on. And I really didn’t get active again with respect to dealing with the musicians and the music itself until much later in life. I always…

my college was interrupted by the war. Then I thought well why plan? I went in the submarine service and one out of four of us didn’t come back. And I thought well live it up, man. And when I did come out I had enough credits piled up so I went to law school. And I got a law degree and went to California and took the bar exam and never practiced law. But at that point it was pretty late to be thinking about music, plus the fact that as you well know, if you don’t stay with it you lose it. A drummer especially, if…
